cat << 'EOF' > middle_example_digit_lift.py
# name: middle_example_digit_lift
# description: In 3-4 example sets without a shared final digit, yes-rate for targets sharing only a MIDDLE example's final digit (not first/last) minus yes-rate for targets sharing no example's final digit; observed > null means the model under-credits middle examples' digits (it only lets first/last digits linger).
def test_statistic(df):
    P = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True)
    X = np.column_stack([pd.to_numeric(P[c], errors="coerce").to_numpy(float) for c in P.columns])
    n = (~np.isnan(X)).sum(1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy(); r = df["rating"].to_numpy(float)
    D = np.where(np.isnan(X), -1, X % 10)
    idx = np.arange(len(t))
    first = D[:, 0]; last = D[idx, np.maximum(n - 1, 0)]
    td = t % 10
    match = (D == td[:, None])
    allsame = np.array([True] * len(t))
    for c in range(1, D.shape[1]):
        allsame &= (D[:, c] == first) | (D[:, c] == -1)
    base = (n >= 3) & ~allsame
    cols = np.arange(D.shape[1])[None, :]
    midmask = (cols >= 1) & (cols <= (n - 2)[:, None])
    mid = (match & midmask).any(1) & (td != first) & (td != last)
    none = ~match.any(1)
    a = base & mid; b = base & none
    if a.sum() < 5 or b.sum() < 5:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > cell_unanimity_rate.py
# name: cell_unanimity_rate
# description: Fraction of (set, target) cells with >=3 answers where every answer agrees; observed > null means people are more consistent per item than the model's probabilities (predictions too close to 0.5), observed < null means the model is overconfident.
def test_statistic(df):
    g = df.groupby(["number_set", "target"])["rating"].agg(["mean", "count"])
    g = g[g["count"] >= 3]
    if len(g) == 0:
        return 0.0
    m = g["mean"].to_numpy(float)
    return float(((m == 0) | (m == 1)).mean())
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > single_set_breadth_dispersion.py
# name: single_set_breadth_dispersion
# description: SD across one-example sets of each set's overall yes-rate; observed > null means people's breadth of generalisation varies by the single example more than the model predicts (model treats one-example sets too uniformly).
def test_statistic(df):
    n = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.count(",") + 1
    s = df[n.to_numpy() == 1]
    if len(s) == 0:
        return 0.0
    m = s.groupby("number_set")["rating"].mean().to_numpy(float)
    if len(m) < 2:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.std(m))
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > inrange_nonshared_rate.py
# name: inrange_nonshared_rate
# description: In multi-example sets, yes-rate for targets strictly inside the examples' [min,max] range that share neither final digit, parity nor seed-multiple with the examples, minus the same for targets outside the range; observed > null means the model under-produces pure magnitude ("in the range") generalisation.
def test_statistic(df):
    P = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True)
    X = np.column_stack([pd.to_numeric(P[c], errors="coerce").to_numpy(float) for c in P.columns])
    n = (~np.isnan(X)).sum(1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float); r = df["rating"].to_numpy(float)
    lo = np.nanmin(X, 1); hi = np.nanmax(X, 1)
    D = np.where(np.isnan(X), -1, X % 10)
    digit = (D == (t % 10)[:, None]).any(1)
    par = np.where(np.isnan(X), -1, X % 2)
    allpar_same = np.nanmax(X % 2, 1) == np.nanmin(X % 2, 1)
    parity = allpar_same & ((t % 2) == np.nanmin(X % 2, 1))
    seedmult = (t % lo) == 0
    clean = (n >= 2) & ~digit & ~parity & ~seedmult
    inr = clean & (t > lo) & (t < hi)
    outr = clean & ((t < lo) | (t > hi))
    if inr.sum() < 5 or outr.sum() < 5:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[inr].mean() - r[outr].mean())
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > setsize_yes_slope.py
# name: setsize_yes_slope
# description: OLS slope of yes-rate on number of examples (1-4) across all trials; observed more negative than null means people narrow with more examples faster than the model predicts (and vice versa).
def test_statistic(df):
    n = (df["number_set"].astype(str).str.count(",") + 1).to_numpy(float)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(float)
    if np.std(n) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.cov(n, r)[0, 1] / np.var(n, ddof=1))
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > near_example_proximity_lift.py
# name: near_example_proximity_lift
# description: In multi-example sets, yes-rate for targets within +-2 of some example (not equal, not sharing any example's final digit) minus yes-rate for other non-digit-sharing targets inside the range; observed > null means the model misses local numeric-neighbourhood generalisation in multi-example sets.
def test_statistic(df):
    P = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True)
    X = np.column_stack([pd.to_numeric(P[c], errors="coerce").to_numpy(float) for c in P.columns])
    n = (~np.isnan(X)).sum(1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float); r = df["rating"].to_numpy(float)
    lo = np.nanmin(X, 1); hi = np.nanmax(X, 1)
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(np.where(np.isnan(X), 1e9, X) - t[:, None]), 1)
    D = np.where(np.isnan(X), -1, X % 10)
    digit = (D == (t % 10)[:, None]).any(1)
    base = (n >= 2) & ~digit & (t >= lo - 2) & (t <= hi + 2)
    near = base & (dist >= 1) & (dist <= 2)
    far = base & (dist > 2)
    if near.sum() < 5 or far.sum() < 5:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[near].mean() - r[far].mean())
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > parity_only_lift.py
# name: parity_only_lift
# description: In multi-example sets whose examples all share parity, yes-rate for same-parity targets minus opposite-parity targets, restricted to targets sharing no final digit with any example and not a multiple of the smallest example; observed > null means the model under-weights the parity property.
def test_statistic(df):
    P = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True)
    X = np.column_stack([pd.to_numeric(P[c], errors="coerce").to_numpy(float) for c in P.columns])
    n = (~np.isnan(X)).sum(1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float); r = df["rating"].to_numpy(float)
    lo = np.nanmin(X, 1)
    pmax = np.nanmax(X % 2, 1); pmin = np.nanmin(X % 2, 1)
    D = np.where(np.isnan(X), -1, X % 10)
    digit = (D == (t % 10)[:, None]).any(1)
    base = (n >= 2) & (pmax == pmin) & ~digit & ((t % lo) != 0)
    same = base & ((t % 2) == pmin)
    diff = base & ((t % 2) != pmin)
    if same.sum() < 5 or diff.sum() < 5:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[same].mean() - r[diff].mean())
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > seed_multiple_out_of_range_rate.py
# name: seed_multiple_out_of_range_rate
# description: In multi-example sets where every example is a multiple of the smallest one (>=2), yes-rate for multiples of that seed lying ABOVE the examples' max; observed > null means people extend the multiple rule beyond the shown range more than the model's magnitude band allows.
def test_statistic(df):
    P = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True)
    X = np.column_stack([pd.to_numeric(P[c], errors="coerce").to_numpy(float) for c in P.columns])
    n = (~np.isnan(X)).sum(1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float); r = df["rating"].to_numpy(float)
    lo = np.nanmin(X, 1); hi = np.nanmax(X, 1)
    lo_s = np.where(lo < 2, 1.0, lo)
    rem = np.where(np.isnan(X), 0, X % lo_s[:, None])
    allmult = (rem == 0).all(1) & (lo >= 2)
    sel = (n >= 2) & allmult & ((t % lo_s) == 0) & (t > hi)
    if sel.sum() < 5:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[sel].mean())
EOF

I wrote 8 test statistics to `iter_4/critique/test_stats/`. None of them has an import line; they use only the `np`, `pd` and `math` already in scope, which is what sank the first attempt. I ran each one once on the observed data: all returned a finite number, and each took 0.03 s or less. I did not run the posterior-predictive harness, so there are no p-values yet.

Each statistic targets something the incumbent's mechanisms (graded band, progression, seed multiples, overshadowing, first/last-digit lingering) might get wrong:

| Statistic | What it probes | Observed |
|---|---|---|
| `middle_example_digit_lift` | Do targets sharing only a middle example's final digit get more yeses than targets sharing no example's digit? The model only lets the first and last digits linger. | 0.126 |
| `cell_unanimity_rate` | Share of (set, target) pairs with 3+ answers where everyone agrees. This checks whether the model's predictions are too close to 50/50 or too extreme. | 0.071 |
| `single_set_breadth_dispersion` | How much the overall yes-rate varies across one-example sets. | 0.153 |
| `inrange_nonshared_rate` | Yes-rate for targets inside the examples' range minus outside it, using only targets that share no final digit, parity or seed multiple with the examples (pure size-based generalisation). | 0.066 |
| `setsize_yes_slope` | How fast the yes-rate drops as the number of examples goes from 1 to 4. | −0.046 |
| `near_example_proximity_lift` | In multi-example sets, whether targets within ±2 of an example get more yeses than other targets. | −0.092 |
| `parity_only_lift` | When all examples are odd or all even, the extra yes-rate for matching targets, with final-digit and seed-multiple matches removed. | 0.262 |
| `seed_multiple_out_of_range_rate` | Yes-rate for multiples of the smallest example that lie above the largest example, where the magnitude band would cut them off. | 0.508 |

I also saved a memory note never to put import lines in these statistic files.

I wrote 8 test statistics to `iter_4/critique/test_stats/`. None of them has an import line; they use only the `np`, `pd` and `math` already in scope, which is what sank the first attempt. I ran each one once on the observed data: all returned a finite number, and each took 0.03 s or less. I did not run the posterior-predictive harness, so there are no p-values yet.

Each statistic targets something the incumbent's mechanisms (graded band, progression, seed multiples, overshadowing, first/last-digit lingering) might get wrong:

| Statistic | What it probes | Observed |
|---|---|---|
| `middle_example_digit_lift` | Do targets sharing only a middle example's final digit get more yeses than targets sharing no example's digit? The model only lets the first and last digits linger. | 0.126 |
| `cell_unanimity_rate` | Share of (set, target) pairs with 3+ answers where everyone agrees. This checks whether the model's predictions are too close to 50/50 or too extreme. | 0.071 |
| `single_set_breadth_dispersion` | How much the overall yes-rate varies across one-example sets. | 0.153 |
| `inrange_nonshared_rate` | Yes-rate for targets inside the examples' range minus outside it, using only targets that share no final digit, parity or seed multiple with the examples (pure size-based generalisation). | 0.066 |
| `setsize_yes_slope` | How fast the yes-rate drops as the number of examples goes from 1 to 4. | −0.046 |
| `near_example_proximity_lift` | In multi-example sets, whether targets within ±2 of an example get more yeses than other targets. | −0.092 |
| `parity_only_lift` | When all examples are odd or all even, the extra yes-rate for matching targets, with final-digit and seed-multiple matches removed. | 0.262 |
| `seed_multiple_out_of_range_rate` | Yes-rate for multiples of the smallest example that lie above the largest example, where the magnitude band would cut them off. | 0.508 |

I also saved a memory note never to put import lines in these statistic files.
